stories.title: Cherokee removal and the Trail of Tears
facts: The Indian Removal Act of 28 May 1830 let the President negotiate treaties to move tribes living east of the Mississippi to land in the west.
https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/jacksons-message-to-congress-on-indian-removal

In December 1835 a small group of Cherokee men, none of them elected officials of the Nation, signed the Treaty of New Echota, giving up all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for $5 million and land in Indian Territory.
https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/cherokee-resistance-and-relocation.htm
Principal Chief John Ross gathered more than 15,000 signatures, nearly the whole Nation, asking the Senate not to ratify it.
https://www.ncpedia.org/cherokee/trailoftears
The Senate ratified the treaty in 1836 by a single vote.
https://www.nps.gov/liri/learn/historyculture/the-trail-of-tears.htm
In May 1838 federal troops and state militias began rounding up Cherokee families into stockades; the forced journey west ran from October 1838 to March 1839.
https://www.nps.gov/liri/learn/historyculture/the-trail-of-tears.htm
More than 16,000 Cherokee people were removed to Indian Territory (now Oklahoma), travelling in 17 detachments along routes of about 2,200 miles.
https://www.nps.gov/places/trail-of-tears-national-historic-trail.htm
A few hundred stayed by hiding in the North Carolina mountains; their descendants are the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.
https://www.ncpedia.org/cherokee/trailoftears

voices.text: But we were doubly grieved when we understood, from a letter of the Secretary of War to our Delegation, dated March of the present year, that our father the President had refused us protection, and that he had decided in favor of the extension of the laws of the State over us. This decision induces us to appeal to the immediate representatives of the American people. We love, we dearly love our country, and it is due to your honorable bodies as well as to us, to make known why we think the country is ours, and why we wish to remain in peace where we are.
voices.who: The Cherokee Nation, memorial to the U.S. Congress
voices.doc: Memorial of the Cherokees

voices.text: By the stipulations of this instrument, we are despoiled of our private possessions, the indefeasible property of individuals. We are stripped of every attribute of freedom and eligibility for legal self-defence. Our property may be plundered before our eyes; violence may be committed on our persons; even our lives may be taken away, and there is none to regard our complaints. We are denationalized; we are disfranchised. We are deprived of membership in the human family! We have neither land nor home, nor resting place that can be called our own. And this is effected by the provisions of a compact which assumes the venerated, the sacred appellation of treaty.
voices.who: Principal Chief John Ross, protest to the Senate and House of Representatives against the Treaty of New Echota
voices.doc: as printed by the U.S. National Park Service

official.text: It gives me pleasure to announce to Congress that the benevolent policy of the Government, steadily pursued for nearly thirty years, in relation to the removal of the Indians beyond the white settlements is approaching to a happy consummation.
official.who: President Andrew Jackson, message to Congress 'On Indian Removal'

disputed: How many died. About 4,000, nearly a fifth of the Cherokee, is the figure most sources give; it goes back to the missionary doctor Elizur Butler. The National Park Service writes that no one knows how many died throughout the ordeal.
stories.blind: Most of what survives is the writing of literate Cherokee leaders, missionaries and army officers. Ordinary Cherokee people, especially women and children and those who spoke only Cherokee, are heard mostly in recollections written down much later.
reading: Trail of Tears National Historic Trail: bibliography (NPS)
Petition against the Treaty of New Echota (National Archives, DocsTeach)

stories.title: Rubber and terror in the Congo Free State
stories.where: Lake Tumba region, Équateur, today's Democratic Republic of the Congo (representative location)
facts: The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 recognised the Congo Free State, ruled personally by King Leopold II of Belgium.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Congo-Free-State
Congolese people were forced to gather wild rubber, palm oil and ivory; families were taken hostage to enforce quotas, and soldiers of the Force Publique cut off hands, including children's.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Congo-Free-State
The British consul Roger Casement travelled the Upper Congo in 1903; his report, dated 11 December 1903, was laid before Parliament in February 1904 as Command Paper Cd. 1933.
https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/50573/pg50573-images.html
Casement and E. D. Morel founded the Congo Reform Association in 1904.
https://breac.nd.edu/articles/the-three-lives-of-the-casement-report-its-impact-on-official-reactions-and-popular-opinion-in-belgium/
The Free State's own Commission of Inquiry, in the Congo from October 1904 to February 1905, confirmed the abuses.
https://breac.nd.edu/articles/the-three-lives-of-the-casement-report-its-impact-on-official-reactions-and-popular-opinion-in-belgium/
Under international pressure Belgium took the territory over in 1908 as the Belgian Congo.
https://breac.nd.edu/articles/the-three-lives-of-the-casement-report-its-impact-on-official-reactions-and-popular-opinion-in-belgium/

voices.text: We had to go further and further into the forest to find the rubber vines, to go without food, and our women had to give up cultivating the fields and gardens. Then we starved. Wild beasts—the leopards—killed some of us when we were working away in the forest, and others got lost or died from exposure and starvation, and we begged the white man to leave us alone, saying we could get no more rubber, but the white men and their soldiers said: ‘Go! You are only beasts yourselves, you are nyama (meat).’ We tried, always going further into the forest, and when we failed and our rubber was short, the soldiers came to our towns and killed us. Many were shot, some had their ears cut off; others were tied up with ropes around their necks and bodies and taken away.
voices.who: A refugee from the rubber tax (named only as “N N” in the published report), speaking to Roger Casement
voices.doc: Correspondence and Report from His Majesty's Consul at Boma (Cd. 1933, 1904), Inclosure 1 in No. 3

voices.text: We said to the white men, ‘We are not enough people now to do what you want us. Our country has not many people in it and we are dying fast. We are killed by the work you make us do, by the stoppage of our plantations, and the breaking up of our homes.’ The white man looked at us and said: ‘There are lots of people in Mputu’
voices.who: Another refugee in the same group (“P P” in the report); Casement notes that Mputu meant Europe
voices.doc: Cd. 1933, Inclosure 1 in No. 3

official.text: They deny, however, that the manner in which the State is administered involves a systematic régime “of cruelty or oppression,”
official.who: The Congo Free State's government: a note to the Powers that signed the Berlin Act, signed by its Secretary-General, Chevalier de Cuvelier, in Brussels (English translation printed in the same Parliamentary paper)

disputed: How many died. Adam Hochschild's widely read estimate is about 10 million, from a population he argues was roughly halved between 1880 and 1920. The demographer Jean-Paul Sanderson told the Belgian Parliament's Congo commission in 2022 that the starting population was probably 11.5 to 15 million, and traced the 10-million figure to Mark Twain's writing in 1908. Administrative counts began in the late 1800s, but Sanderson considers them reliable only from about 1935.

Deaths or decline. Sanderson attributes the fall mainly to higher mortality and lower birth rates, from violence, flight, famine and diseases such as sleeping sickness, and stresses that the gap measures decline, not violent deaths alone; Britannica reports a decline said to be from some 20 million to 8 million.
stories.blind: Congolese voices survive only as answers given to European questioners, through interpreters, and printed with names removed. The dead, most women, and people who never met a missionary or consul are almost entirely missing.
reading: The three lives of the Casement Report (University of Notre Dame, Breac)

stories.title: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre
facts: On 13 April 1919 troops under General Dyer fired on a large unarmed crowd in the Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden in Amritsar; Dyer reported that his party fired 1,650 rounds.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1920/jul/19/punjab-disturbances-the-case-of-general
In the House of Commons the Secretary for War, Winston Churchill, gave the official toll as 379 killed and at least 1,200 wounded, and called it a monstrous event.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1920/jul/08/army-council-and-general-dyer
Martial law followed in the Punjab, enforced with public floggings and other humiliations; Rabindranath Tagore gave up the knighthood he had received in 1915.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Jallianwala-Bagh-Massacre

The government's Disorders Inquiry (Hunter) Committee condemned General Dyer's conduct; on 8 July 1920 the Commons rejected, by 230 votes to 129, Sir Edward Carson's motion protesting at his treatment.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1920/jul/08/army-council-and-general-dyer
On 20 July 1920 the House of Lords voted 129 to 86 for a motion deploring the handling of General Dyer's case as unjust to him.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1920/jul/20/punjab-disturbances-the-case-of-general

voices.text: The enormity of the measures taken by the Government in the Punjab for quelling some local disturbances has, with a rude shock, revealed to our minds the helplessness of our position as British subjects in India. The disproportionate severity of the punishments inflicted upon the unfortunate people and the methods of carrying them out, we are convinced, are without parallel in the history of civilised governments, barring some conspicuous exceptions, recent and remote. Considering that such treatment has been meted out to a population, disarmed and resourceless, by a power which has the most terribly efficient organisation for destruction of human lives, we must strongly assert that it can claim no political expediency, far less moral justification.
voices.who: Rabindranath Tagore, letter to the Viceroy giving up his knighthood
voices.doc: as reprinted by Mainstream Weekly

official.text: Did the crowd at once start to disperse as soon as you fired? (A.) Immediately. (Q.) Did you continue firing? (A.) Yes. (Q.) If the crowd was going to disperse why did you not stop firing? (A.) I thought it my duty to go on firing until it dispersed. If I fired a little the effect would not be sufficient.
official.who: General R. E. H. Dyer, who gave the order to fire, questioned by the government's Disorders Inquiry (Hunter) Committee (as read out in the House of Lords)
official.date: evidence of 1919; read in the Lords on 19 July 1920

official.text: In continuing firing as long as he did it is evident that General Dyer had in view not merely the dispersal of the crowd that had assembled contrary to his orders, but the desire to produce a moral effect in the Punjab.
official.who: Majority report of the Hunter Committee, as quoted in the House of Lords (it goes on to call this a misconception of his duty)

disputed: How many were killed. The official British figure is 379. The Indian National Congress inquiry wrote that 1,000 was no exaggeration; other contemporary estimates ran from about 500 to over 1,000, and the historian Kim Wagner puts it between 500 and 600.
Whether the crowd was warned. The Hunter Committee held that notice to disperse should have been given; Dyer's defenders in the Lords argued that earlier proclamations were warning enough.
stories.blind: Most of the dead and wounded were never named in the record; they appear as numbers, and the story is told mainly through officials, commissions and famous protesters rather than the people in the garden.
reading: Jallianwala Bagh at 100: how many actually died (The Week)

stories.title: Peterloo
facts: On 16 August 1819 a meeting on St Peter's Field, Manchester, called by the Manchester Patriotic Union to demand votes for all men and fairer representation, was broken up by cavalry.
https://historyofparliament.com/2013/10/15/peterloo-and-its-aftermath/
The Manchester and Salford Yeomanry and the 15th Hussars were sent into a crowd of more than 60,000.
https://historyofparliament.com/2019/08/16/protest-against-the-six-acts/
The University of Manchester counts 18 people who died of injuries received that afternoon and up to 700 injured; the name Peterloo mocked the Battle of Waterloo four years earlier.
https://www.digitalcollections.manchester.ac.uk/collections/peterloo
The speaker, Henry Hunt, was charged with high treason, later reduced to sedition, and jailed for 30 months.
https://historyofparliament.com/2013/10/15/peterloo-and-its-aftermath/
By the end of 1819 Parliament had passed the Six Acts, restricting public meetings, arms and the radical press.
https://historyofparliament.com/2019/08/16/protest-against-the-six-acts/
John Edward Taylor, who was there and served on the committee for the victims' relief, founded the Manchester Guardian, first published on 5 May 1821.
https://www.digitalcollections.manchester.ac.uk/view/AR-GDN-00150-00001

voices.text: The cavalry were in confusion: they evidently could not, with all the weight of man and horse, penetrate that compact mass of human beings; and their sabres were plied to hew a way through naked held-up hands and defenceless heads; and then chopped limbs and wound-gaping skulls were seen; and groans and cries were mingled with the din of that horrid confusion.
voices.who: Samuel Bamford, a weaver from Middleton who led his town's contingent that day
voices.doc: Passages in the Life of a Radical, 1893 edition, p. 156 (transcribed from the scan; line-break hyphens joined)

voices.text: Many females appeared as the crowd opened; and striplings or mere youths also were found. Their cries were piteous and heart-rending, and would, one might have supposed, have disarmed any human resentment: but here their appeals were in vain. Women, white-vested maids, and tender youths, were indiscriminately sabred or trampled; and we have reason for believing that few were the instances in which that forbearance was vouchsafed which they so earnestly implored.
voices.who: Samuel Bamford
voices.doc: Passages in the Life of a Radical, 1893 edition, p. 156 (transcribed from the scan)

official.text: the seditious practices so long prevalent in some of the manufacturing districts of the country have been continued with increased activity since you were last assembled in parliament.
official.who: The Prince Regent's speech opening Parliament, which went on to call for measures to suppress them (the Six Acts); it did not mention Peterloo by name

disputed: How many were killed and hurt. The History of Parliament says at least 11 dead and 400–600 injured; UNESCO UK says at least 15 killed and 700 seriously injured; the University of Manchester says 18 dead and up to 700 injured, and that the magistrates' version seriously downplayed the casualties.
How big the crowd was: estimates run from about 60,000 to 80,000.
stories.blind: Most crowd testimony comes from men speaking in court or writing for reform. The many women at the meeting, and the injured too poor or afraid to claim relief, survive mostly as names and injury notes in the relief fund's records.
reading: Peterloo Relief Fund account book (UNESCO UK Memory of the World)

stories.title: The Myall Creek massacre
stories.where: Myall Creek, near Bingara, New South Wales, Australia (memorial site)
facts: On 10 June 1838 a group of armed stockmen rode onto Myall Creek station and killed Wirrayaraay women, children and old men of the Gamilaraay nation.
https://myallcreek.org/the-massacre-story/
The remains of at least 28 people were later seen at the site; the full death toll has never been confirmed.
https://nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/myall-creek-massacre
At the first trial, on 15 November 1838, all 11 accused men were found not guilty.
https://nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/myall-creek-massacre
At a second trial, begun on 29 November 1838, seven men were found guilty and sentenced to death; they were hanged in Sydney on 18 December 1838.
https://nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/myall-creek-massacre
The man who led the attack, John Fleming, was never tried.
https://mhnsw.au/stories/general/myall-creek-massacre/
On 10 June 2000 Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Australians opened a memorial at the site; it joined the National Heritage List in 2008.
https://apps.environment.nsw.gov.au/dpcheritageapp/ViewHeritageItemDetails.aspx?ID=5056626

voices.text: the mothers and children were crying, and the little ones that could not walk; Russel brought out he end of the rope that they were tied with, and gave it to one of the men on horseback; they then started, taking the blacks with them; the man who took the rope from Russel went in front; they were tied; one black was handcuffed; their hands were all tied, with the palms to each other; the rope was a very long one; they took all the blacks away, except two boys that jumped into the creek as the men were coming up
voices.who: George Anderson, the station's hut-keeper, giving evidence at the first trial
voices.date: 15 November 1838 (reported in the Sydney Gazette, 20 November 1838)
voices.doc: R. v. Kilmeister (No. 1) [1838] NSWSupC 105, Macquarie Law School (archived copy; the live site was not answering)

voices.text: There was here no provocation; no cause for anger. Men, women, children, even babes hanging at their mothers' breasts, not less than 30 altogether of these unfortunate defenceless blacks, who were quietly reposing by their evening fire, believing themselves safe in the friendship of one of you, were suddenly surrounded by a party of horsemen
voices.who: Justice William Burton, passing sentence on the seven men
voices.date: 5 December 1838 (reported in the Sydney Gazette, 6 December 1838)
voices.doc: R. v. Kilmeister (No. 2) [1838] NSWSupC 110, Macquarie Law School (archived copy)

disputed: How many were killed: at least 28 (National Museum of Australia), “not less than 30” (the judge in 1838), with victims' names still not fully known.

The size of the party and who escaped justice: at least 10 and possibly 12 stockmen (Friends of Myall Creek); ten besides its leader (Museums of History NSW). The leader, John Fleming, was never caught; four of the accused were never retried; the same party is reported to have killed 30 to 40 more people nearby.
stories.warn: The 1838 words are kept exactly as printed, including terms that are now offensive.
stories.blind: The record is almost entirely what white men said in court and wrote in the press. Aboriginal people could not then give sworn evidence, so the survivors and the victims' families are missing from it, and most of the dead are still unnamed.
reading: The massacre story (Friends of Myall Creek)
Myall Creek massacre (National Museum of Australia)

press.text: The whole gang of black animals are not worth the money which the Colonists will have to pay for printing the very documents upon which we have already wasted too much time.
press.who: The Sydney Herald, editorial on the colony's new protectors of Aborigines, written while the Myall Creek accused awaited trial (the newspaper, now the Sydney Morning Herald, apologised in 2023)

stories.title: The Armenian genocide
stories.where: Harput (today Elazığ), one of the towns deportations began from (approximate)
facts: On 24 April 1915 the Ottoman government arrested about 250 Armenian intellectuals and political leaders in Constantinople (Istanbul).
https://www.britannica.com/event/Armenian-Genocide
The U.S. ambassador, Henry Morgenthau, reported on 27 April 1915 that more than a hundred Armenians had been arrested and were being sent into the interior.
https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1915Supp/d1395
Armenians across Anatolia were deported toward the Syrian desert; many of those who reached it were held in camps where they starved, and massacres continued into 1916.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Armenian-Genocide
On 24 May 1915 the Allied governments warned that they would hold every member of the Ottoman government personally responsible for what they called new crimes against humanity and civilization.
https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1915Supp/d1398
In 2019 the U.S. House of Representatives passed a resolution commemorating the killing of 1.5 million Armenians from 1915 to 1923.
https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-resolution/296
On 24 April 2021 the U.S. President formally used the words Armenian genocide in his annual remembrance statement.
https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/24/statement-by-president-joe-biden-on-armenian-remembrance-day/

voices.text: All the people of C. started the same day. I think we were about 600 families. We had with us all our cattle and all our property. The first night we reached AU. and slept that night in the fields. The next day we passed many corpses heaped together under bridges and on the road; their blood had collected in pools.
voices.who: An Armenian woman deported from the Harput region on 4 July 1915 (unnamed in the publication; towns are shown only as letters)
voices.doc: Bryce and Toynbee (eds.), The Treatment of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire, 1915–16 (1916), Doc. 68

today.text: Türkiye does not deny the suffering of Armenians, including the loss of many innocent lives, during the First World War. However, greater numbers of Turks died or were killed in the years leading to and during the War.
today.who: Republic of Türkiye, Ministry of Foreign Affairs (the Ottoman government's own words from 1915 were not found in a source we could check)
today.date: as published on its website (checked November 2026)

disputed: How many died. Britannica gives conservative estimates of 600,000 to more than 1,000,000; the 2019 House resolution and the 2021 presidential statement say 1.5 million.

Whether it was genocide. Turkey's government says Armenians were relocated away from a war zone during a fight for survival, that deaths came from wartime conditions, disease, famine and banditry, and that there is no authentic evidence of a plan; it calls the genocide label legally unfounded. The United States and many other governments call it genocide, and Britannica says most historians have concluded that it fits the definition. Morgenthau cabled in July 1915 of a 'systematic attempt to uproot peaceful Armenian populations.'
stories.blind: The best-known survivor accounts were published by wartime Britain with names hidden; the Ottoman archives, and Turkish and Kurdish civilians' own experience of those years, are largely absent from these sources.
reading: The Treatment of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire (Project Gutenberg)
U.S. diplomatic records, 1915 (Office of the Historian)

witness.text: Persecution of Armenians assuming unprecedented proportions. Reports from widely scattered districts indicate systematic attempt to uproot peaceful Armenian populations and through arbitrary arrests, terrible tortures, wholesale expulsions and deportations from one end of the Empire to the other accompanied by frequent instances of rape, pillage, and murder, turning into massacre, to bring destruction and destitution on them.
witness.who: Henry Morgenthau, U.S. ambassador in Constantinople, telegram to the Secretary of State

stories.title: The Herero and Nama genocide
facts: The war in German South West Africa began on 12 January 1904 at Okahandja.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
On 11 August 1904 at the Waterberg, about 1,500 German troops under General Lothar von Trotha attacked an estimated 40,000 Herero, about 5,000 of them armed.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
Most Herero fled into the Kalahari toward British Bechuanaland; German patrols guarded the desert's edge, and many thousands died of thirst.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
Survivors were held in concentration camps; up to 80 percent of the prisoners on Shark Island, near Lüderitz, are estimated to have died there.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
On 28 May 2021 Germany's Foreign Minister said Germany would officially call the events a genocide and pledged €1.1 billion, stating that no legal claims for compensation follow from it.
https://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/en/newsroom/news/-/2463598

voices.text: We were crushed and well-nigh exterminated by the Germans in the rising. With the exception of Samuel Maharero, Mutati, Traugott, Tjetjoo, Hosea and Kaijata (who fled to British territory) all our big chiefs and leaders died or were killed in the rising, and also the great majority of our people. All our cattle were lost and all other possessions such as wagons and sheep. At first the Germans took prisoners, but when General von Trotha took command no prisoners were taken. General von Trotha said, ‘No one is to live; men, women and children must all die.’ We can't say how many were killed.
voices.who: Hosea Mungunda, headman of the Herero at Windhoek, statement
voices.doc: Report on the Natives of South-West Africa and their Treatment by Germany (Cd. 9146, 1918)

voices.text: In 1906 the Germans took me a prisoner after we had made peace, and sent me with about a thousand other Hottentots to Aus, thence to Luderitzbucht, and finally to Shark Island. We were placed on the island, men, women, and children. We were beaten daily by the Germans, who used sjamboks. They were most cruel to us. We lived in tents on the island; food, blankets, and lashes were given to us in plenty, and the young girls were violated at night by the guards. Six months later we went by boat to Swakopmund, and thence by train to Karibib. Lots of my people died on Shark Island.
voices.who: Edward Fredericks, headman of the Bethany Nama, sworn statement
voices.doc: Cd. 9146 (1918), transcribed from the scan

official.text: Any Herero found within the German frontier, with or without a gun, with or without cattle, will be shot. I spare neither women nor children—I drive them back to their people or I will fire upon them.
official.who: General Lothar von Trotha's proclamation to the Herero (English translation by David Ciarlo, German History in Documents and Images; original in the German Federal Archives)

disputed: How many died. Britannica says about 75 percent of the Herero and half of the Nama; the BBC says up to 80 percent of the indigenous populations; the 1918 report put it at 60,000 or more.

The 2021 agreement. Germany calls its €1.1 billion a gesture of recognition with no legal claims attached and says Herero and Nama representatives were closely involved in the talks; a Herero activist told the BBC the offer was not enough, and a historian said many descendants felt excluded.
stories.warn: The 1918 words are kept as printed, including terms that are now offensive.
stories.blind: Nearly all the survivor testimony was gathered by a British wartime administration that wanted to keep the territory, and reached print in English through interpreters; women's and San survivors' voices are few.
reading: Samuel Maharero's letter to Governor Leutwein, 1904 (GHDI)

stories.title: The Bengal famine of 1943
facts: The government's Famine Inquiry Commission estimated some 1.5 million deaths above the normal level in 1943 and the first half of 1944.
https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.206311
Britannica puts the toll at some three million people, dead of malnutrition or disease.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bengal-famine-of-1943
Rice imports stopped after Japan took Burma in 1942, and a cyclone in October 1942 damaged the autumn rice crop, though Britannica says these events had a relatively minor impact on the food supply.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bengal-famine-of-1943
Under a military denial policy in 1942, rice and paddy judged surplus were removed from the coastal districts of Midnapore, Bakarganj and Khulna.
https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.206311
In the House of Commons on 4 November 1943, the Labour MP Frederick Pethick-Lawrence blamed inflation, saying food-grain prices had risen by 100 to 700 percent.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1943/nov/04/india-food-situation
The economist Amartya Sen, who saw the famine as a boy, later described it as an entitlement failure: people could not afford food, rather than there being too little food overall.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bengal-famine-of-1943

official.text: The cyclone and the partial failure of the aman crop were serious and unavoidable natural calamities. But after considering all the circumstances, we cannot avoid the conclusion that it lay in the power of the Government of Bengal, by bold, resolute and well-conceived measures at the right time to have largely prevented the tragedy of the famine as it actually took place.
official.who: Famine Inquiry Commission, the government's own inquiry, Report on Bengal (transcribed from the scan; three scanning errors corrected)

official.text: Meanwhile, the tragic tale of loss of life has continued and is still continuing. The death rate directly or indirectly due to starvation, for Calcutta alone, has amounted to some 8,000 between 15th August and 15th October. There are no reliable figures available for the outside districts, but I fear that in South-West and South-East Bengal, the figures may have been even worse than those in Calcutta. Even now that sufficient outside supplies for the Province seem assured, there will be for some time no diminution in the loss of life, until the organisation of distribution has effectively covered the whole ground.
official.who: Leo Amery, Secretary of State for India, in the House of Commons

official.text: The problem before them has throughout been one of high prices and of local shortage, both essentially due to maldistribution rather than to an absolute over-all total shortage for the whole of India.
official.who: Leo Amery, Secretary of State for India, on the Government of India's task, House of Commons

disputed: How many died, and how reliable the official record is. The Commission estimated about 1.5 million; other estimates run to about 3 million. The historian Madhusree Mukerjee, comparing the Commission's unpublished hearings with its report, found serious omissions in its rice-supply figures.

Nature or policy. A 2019 study of India's famines found that five of six major ones were linked to drought, but not 1943; the economic historian Tirthankar Roy argues that focusing on 1943 gives a skewed view of imperial responsibility and weighs climate and environment more heavily.
stories.blind: Most deaths were in villages where nobody counted them; the Commission judged the recorded figures an under-estimate, by about 40 percent for 1943. The famine's victims are almost silent in the official record: this card has no first-hand account from them yet, and we are still looking for one we can quote.
reading: Mukerjee, The Bengal Famine of 1943: An Appraisal of the Famine Inquiry Commission (EPW, 2014)

stories.title: The Highland Clearances
facts: The Clearances were forced evictions in the Scottish Highlands from the later 1700s into the mid-1800s, mainly to make way for sheep farming.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Highland-Clearances
On the Sutherland estates, around 1810 to 1820, thousands of families were evicted and resettled on coastal crofts to gather kelp or fish.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Highland-Clearances
In June 1814 the estate factor Patrick Sellar cleared the townships of a Strathnaver farm he was taking over himself.
https://www.communitylandscotland.org.uk/resources/jim-hunter-reflects-on-the-200-year-anniversary-of-the-trial-of-patrick-sellar/
Sellar was tried for culpable homicide at Inverness in April 1816 and found not guilty.
https://www.communitylandscotland.org.uk/resources/jim-hunter-reflects-on-the-200-year-anniversary-of-the-trial-of-patrick-sellar/
After the potato blight of the 1840s many Highlanders emigrated to the Lowlands, Canada, the United States and Australia, some with passages paid by landlords.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Highland-Clearances

The Napier Commission, appointed in 1883, heard about 800 people at 61 places; the Crofters Holdings Act of 1886 then limited evictions and brought in fair rents and secure tenancy for crofters, though not for landless cottars.
https://www.highlifehighland.com/archives/highland-archive-service/online-exhibitions/the-battle-of-the-braes/the-napier-commission

voices.text: I was present at the pulling down and burning of the house of William Chisholm, Badinloskin, in which was lying his wife's mother, an old bed-ridden woman of near 100 years of age, none of the family being present. I informed the persons about to set fire to the house of this circumstance, and prevailed on them to wait till Mr. Sellar came. On his arrival I told him of the poor old woman being in a condition unfit for removal. He replied, "Damn her, the old witch, she has lived too long; let her burn." Fire was immediately set to the house, and the blankets in which she was carried were in flames before she could be got out. She was placed in a little shed, and it was with great difficulty they were prevented from firing it also.
voices.who: Donald MacLeod, a Strathnaver stonemason, describing the 1814 clearance decades later (one witness's account; Sellar was tried over these evictions and acquitted)
voices.doc: Gloomy Memories in the Highlands of Scotland (transcribed from the scan)

official.text: So decided, indeed, has this progress been, and so much superior has the new system shown itself to be, in every point of view; especially in the manner in which it has influenced the habits of the people; that some parts of the arrangements have been executed to a greater extent than it was possible to contemplate at their commencement.
official.who: James Loch, commissioner of the Sutherland estates, An Account of the Improvements on the Estates of the Marquess of Stafford (the estate's own published account)

disputed: Eviction or emigration. The historian James Hunter describes about 200 long-settled Sutherland communities destroyed by eviction; Eric Richards and others define clearance more broadly, including voluntary departure, and recent scholarship differs significantly from John Prebble's 1963 account of Highlanders forced into exile by chiefs turned landlords.
stories.blind: Almost all the evicted people's words reach us in English, through interpreters, clerks or later campaigners; very little survives in their own Gaelic, in their own hand.
reading: The Napier Commission (High Life Highland archives)

stories.title: The Nakba: the Palestinian exodus of 1947–49
stories.where: Lydda (Lod), whose fall in July 1948 the UN mediator named as the point the refugee crisis became acute
facts: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181, recommending that Palestine be divided into a Jewish state and an Arab state.
https://www.britannica.com/event/1948-Arab-Israeli-War
The Zionist Organization approved the partition resolution; Arab leaders opposed it.
https://www.un.org/unispal/history2/origins-and-evolution-of-the-palestine-problem/part-ii-1947-1977/
A civil war followed the vote; by mid-May 1948 some 250,000–300,000 Palestinian Arabs had left or been expelled from their homes.
https://www.britannica.com/event/1948-Arab-Israeli-War
Israel declared its independence on 14 May 1948; the next day the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon invaded, carrying out a decision the Arab League had made weeks before.
https://www.britannica.com/event/1948-Arab-Israeli-War
In July 1948 Israeli forces took Lydda (Lod) and Ramla, towns inside the partition plan's proposed Arab state.
https://www.britannica.com/event/1948-Arab-Israeli-War
The UN study The Origins and Evolution of the Palestine Problem puts the number of refugees at 726,000 by the end of 1949, about half the Arab population of Palestine.
https://www.un.org/unispal/history2/origins-and-evolution-of-the-palestine-problem/part-ii-1947-1977/

On 11 December 1948 the General Assembly resolved, in Resolution 194, that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date, with compensation paid for the property of those choosing not to return.
https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-177019/
In December 1949 the General Assembly set up UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestine refugees.
https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-180266/
Armistice agreements with Egypt, Lebanon, Transjordan and Syria between February and July 1949 ended the war and set de facto borders.
https://www.britannica.com/event/1948-Arab-Israeli-War

witness.text: It is, however, undeniable that no settlement can be just and complete if recognition is not accorded to the right of the Arab refugee to return to the home from which he has been dislodged by the hazards and strategy of the armed conflict between Arabs and Jews in Palestine. The majority of these refugees have come from territory which, under the Assembly resolution of 29 November, was to be included in the Jewish State. The exodus of Palestinian Arabs resulted from panic created by fighting in their communities, by rumours concerning real or alleged acts of terrorism, or expulsion. It would be an offence against the principles of elemental justice if these innocent victims of the conflict were denied the right to return to their homes while Jewish immigrants flow into Palestine, and, indeed, at least offer the threat of permanent replacement of the Arab refugees who have been rooted in the land for centuries.
witness.who: Count Folke Bernadotte, UN Mediator on Palestine, Progress Report to the General Assembly (A/648), signed at Rhodes

witness.text: This situation reached an acute stage owing to the fact that just before the second truce (18 July 1948) Ramleh and Lydda, to which many thousands had fled from Jaffa and other localities, also fell. Moreover, while those who had fled in the early days of the conflict had been able to take with them some personal effects and assets, many of the late-comers were deprived of everything except the cloths in which they stood, and apart from their homes (many of which were destroyed) lost all furniture and assets, and even their tools of trade.
witness.who: The same report, on the refugees' conditions ("cloths" as printed)

official.text: If the war has brought in its wake a mass exodus, mostly spontaneous and the exodus has resulted in great suffering, the responsibility for it rests on those who fomented and have carried on the war, as well as on those who aided and abetted them.
official.who: Provisional Government of Israel, reply to the UN Mediator (S/949), printed as an annex to his report; it added that Israel could not re-admit the refugees on any substantial scale while a state of war existed

disputed: Why they left. Israel's government in 1948 called the exodus mostly spontaneous and blamed those who started the war; Britannica notes that in Tiberias, Haifa and Safed Arabs fled despite Jewish authorities urging them to stay. The historian Benny Morris, working from Israeli archives, concludes that war and not design, Jewish or Arab, gave birth to the refugee problem, while writing that displacement was inherent in Zionist thinking. A study for the UN committee set up to promote Palestinian rights stresses terror and expulsion and rejects the charge that Arab leaders incited the flight. Palestinian historians' own accounts are not yet quoted on this card.

How many. Estimates of the Arabs displaced from December 1947 to January 1949 range from about 520,000 to about 1,000,000; Britannica notes a general consensus that the number was more than 600,000 and likely exceeded 700,000.
stories.note: Research in progress (4 Nov 2026): this card has no refugees' own words yet. The quotations come from UN documents, quoted briefly with credit; the UN's terms cover personal, non-commercial use.
stories.blind: The 1948 record quoted here is the voice of the UN and governments; the refugees themselves, and the Jewish communities attacked in the same war, are not yet heard in their own words on this card.
reading: Benny Morris, The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited (Cambridge), conclusion

stories.title: The Great Irish Famine
facts: In 1845 potato blight reached Ireland and much of that year's crop rotted; the failures of 1846 to 1849 were worse.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history
About one million people died of starvation, typhus or other famine-related disease, and emigration during the famine may have reached two million.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history
Ireland's population fell from almost 8.4 million in 1844 to 6.6 million in 1851.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history
Grain went on being exported from Ireland to Britain during the famine; Peel's government allowed it, and Russell's government after it kept the same policy.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history
By August 1847 as many as three million people were receiving soup-kitchen rations; with public works, government relief cost about £8 million.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history

official.text: The deep and inveterate root of social evil remained, and this has been laid bare by a direct stroke of an all-wise and all-merciful Providence, as if this part of the case were beyond the unassisted power of man.
official.who: Charles Trevelyan, Assistant Secretary to the Treasury, who ran famine relief, The Irish Crisis

disputed: Neglect or something worse. In 1861 the nationalist John Mitchel wrote that the Almighty sent the potato blight but the English created the Famine, and some writers since have called British policy genocidal; the majority of historians of the subject reject the genocide charge, while many, among them Christine Kinealy, fault the government's response and write that it used the crisis to push through long-desired changes in Ireland.

Food exports. Cecil Woodham-Smith called continued exports an indisputable fact that embittered relations; others point out that Ireland became a net importer of grain from 1847, bringing in several times more wheat than it sent out at the height of the famine.
stories.blind: The voices that survive belong mostly to outsiders writing in English; the starving, many of whom spoke Irish and could not write, rarely left records of their own, and the official death tables are known to undercount.
reading: O'Rourke, The History of the Great Irish Famine of 1847 (Project Gutenberg)
Nicholson, Annals of the Famine in Ireland (scan)

witness.text: A servant in the house where I was stopping, at Kingstown, said that the milk woman wished me to see a man near by, that was in a state of actual starvation; and he was going out to attempt to work on the Queen's highway; a little labor was beginning opposite the house, and fifteen-pence a-day stimulated this poor man, who had seven to support, his rent to pay, and fuel to buy. He had been sick with fever; the clothes of his family that would fetch any price, had been pawned or sold, and all were starving together. He staggered with his spade to the work; the overseer objected; but he entreated to be allowed to try.
witness.who: Asenath Nicholson, an American who walked Ireland during the famine
witness.doc: Annals of the Famine in Ireland, p. 37 (transcribed from the scan)

witness.text: In this town have I witnessed to-day, men--fathers, carrying perhaps their only child to its last home, its remains enclosed in a few deal boards patched together; I have seen them, on this day, in three or four instances, carrying those coffins under their arms or upon their shoulders, without a single individual in attendance upon them; without mourner or ceremony--without wailing or lamentation. The people in the street, the labourers congregated in town, regarded the spectacle without surprise; they looked on with indifference, because it was of hourly occurrence.
witness.who: The Cork Examiner's special correspondent in Skibbereen, as quoted by John O'Rourke
witness.doc: O'Rourke, The History of the Great Irish Famine of 1847 (1902 ed.)

stories.note: Research in progress: this card has no famine victim's own words yet.

stories.title: Slavery in the United States, in the words of the formerly enslaved
stories.where: Little Rock, Arkansas, where Jeff Bailey was interviewed in 1938
facts: The 1860 census counted 3,953,760 enslaved people out of about 31.4 million Americans.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_United_States_census
The 13th Amendment, passed by Congress on 31 January 1865 and ratified on 6 December 1865, abolished slavery in the United States, except as punishment for a crime.
https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/13th-amendment
Between 1936 and 1938 the Federal Writers' Project recorded about 2,300 first-person accounts of slavery, now held by the Library of Congress.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WPA_Slave_Narrative_Collection
The project's editors in Washington told interviewers how to spell Black speech, and most interviewers were white, working in the segregated South.
https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/13847
Many of the people interviewed had been children under slavery: Jeff Bailey, born in 1861, was a small child at emancipation.
https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11255

voices.text: I seed slaves for sale on de auction block. They sol' 'em 'cordin' to strengt' and muscles. They was stripped to de wais'. I seed the women and little chillun cryin' and beggin' not to be separated, but it didn' do no good. They had to go.
voices.who: Stearlin Arnwine, aged 94, near Jacksonville, Texas
voices.doc: Slave Narratives, Vol. XVI, Texas Narratives, Part 1

voices.text: I remember what they said when they freed my father. They said, 'You're free. You children are free. Go on back there and work and let your children work. Don't work them children too long. You'll git pay for your work.' That was in the Monticello courthouse yard. They said, 'You're free! Free!'
voices.who: Jeff Bailey, born in Monticello, Arkansas in 1861, interviewed in Little Rock by Samuel S. Taylor
voices.doc: Slave Narratives, Vol. II, Arkansas Narratives, Part 1

stories.warn: Many interviewers wrote speech in dialect spellings, on which the project's editors gave guidance; the words are kept exactly as recorded.

official.text: Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery-- the greatest material interest of the world. Its labor supplies the product which constitutes by far the largest and most important portions of commerce of the earth.
official.who: Mississippi, Declaration of the Immediate Causes which Induce and Justify the Secession of the State of Mississippi from the Federal Union

disputed: How far the narratives can be trusted. The collection's 1941 editor, B. A. Botkin, warned of bias, faulty memory and leading questions yet called it the most authentic source on enslaved people's lives; the historian John Blassingame warned that it can give a simplistic and distorted view of the plantation, and others argue that people speaking to white interviewers in the Jim Crow South kept a mask of civility.
stories.blind: These are formerly enslaved people's own memories, but mostly white government interviewers chose the questions, decided how speech was spelled and edited the typescripts, and many speakers were recalling childhood seventy years before.
reading: Born in Slavery: Slave Narratives from the Federal Writers' Project (Library of Congress)

stories.title: The Haitian Revolution and the price of independence
stories.where: Gonaïves, Haiti, where independence was declared
facts: In August 1791 thousands of enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in rebellion.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Haitian-Revolution
In 1793 the French commissioner Sonthonax abolished slavery in the colony, and the French government confirmed it the following year.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Haitian-Revolution
Toussaint Louverture agreed to an armistice in May 1802, was imprisoned in France despite it, and died there on 7 April 1803.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Haitian-Revolution
On 1 January 1804 the former French colony of Saint-Domingue was declared independent under the name Haiti.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Haitian-Revolution
From February to April 1804, on Jean-Jacques Dessalines's orders, Haitian soldiers killed most of the French who remained, between 3,000 and 7,000 people.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1804_Haitian_massacre
To pay the first instalment of a 150-million-franc indemnity demanded by France in 1825, Haiti borrowed 30 million francs; the bankers kept 6 million as commission.
https://github.com/nytimes/haiti-debt
An 1838 treaty cut the total to 90 million francs; Haiti made its last indemnity payment in 1878 and said in 1887 that it had paid off the loan.
https://github.com/nytimes/haiti-debt

voices.text: behold this land which we have watered with our sweat—or rather, with our blood,—those edifices which we have raised, and that in the hope of a just reward! Have we obtained it? The King—the whole World—has bewailed our lot, and broken our chains; while, on our part, we, humble victims, were ready for anything, not wishing to abandon our masters. What do we say? We are mistaken; those who, next to God, should have proved our fathers, have been tyrants, monsters unworthy of the fruits of our labours: and do you, brave general, desire that as sheep we should throw ourselves into the jaws of the wolf? No! it is too late.
voices.who: The insurgent leaders under Jean-François, replying to the colony's governor
voices.doc: English text in John R. Beard, The Life of Toussaint L'Ouverture (1853), transcribed from the scan

voices.text: Requested the Generals to swear to abjure forever allegiance to France, to die rather than to live under her domination, and to fight to the last for the preservation of their independence. The Generals imbued with these sacred principles, after proclaiming in a loud voice their unanimous adhesion to the resolution of independence, swore for all their posterity and to the world to abjure forever allegiance to France, and to die rather than to live under her domination.
voices.who: The Act of Independence signed at Gonaïves by Jean-Jacques Dessalines and his generals
voices.doc: English text in J. N. Léger, Haiti: Her History and Her Detractors (1907)

official.text: Les habitans actuels de là partie française de Saint-Domingue verseront à la caisse générale des dépôts et consignations de France, en cinq termes égaux, d'année en année, le premier échéant au 31 décembre 1825, la somme de cent cinquante millions de francs, destinée à dédommager les anciens colons qui réclameront une indemnité.
official.who: King Charles X's ordinance recognising Haiti, Article 2, in the original French as reproduced by Beaubrun Ardouin (in short: the inhabitants must pay France 150 million francs in five yearly instalments to compensate the former colonists)

disputed: What the indemnity cost Haiti. A 2022 New York Times analysis estimated $21 billion to $115 billion in lost growth over two centuries; other economists have built their own long-run estimates of Haiti's debt burden, and the figure depends heavily on assumptions about growth.
How many died in the war. J. N. Léger wrote in 1907 of over 50,000 French dead; modern estimates run to about 200,000 Haitian and 57,000 to 75,000 French dead, all uncertain.
stories.blind: Almost every surviving text of the revolution comes from leaders and their secretaries writing in French; the enslaved majority, most of them born in Africa and speaking Kreyòl, reach us mainly through others.
reading: The New York Times debt data and method
Beard, The Life of Toussaint L'Ouverture (scan)

stories.title: Kenya's Emergency and the detention camps
facts: In October 1952 the British colonial government of Kenya declared a state of emergency, which was not lifted until 1960.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mau-Mau
The BBC reports that some 150,000 Kenyans went through 'screening' and more than 1,000 were sent to the gallows.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-13044974
Mau Mau fighters also killed civilians: 1,819 Africans by the official count, which the historian David Anderson puts nearer 5,000, as well as 32 European and 26 Asian civilians.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_rebellion
At Hola camp in March 1959, eleven detainees died after being beaten; members of the House of Commons debated the deaths that July.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1959/jul/27/hola-camp-kenya-report
In April 2011 a High Court case brought out more than 17,000 pages of colonial files that had been held in secret at the Foreign Office's Hanslope Park.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-13044974
In June 2013 the British government settled with 5,228 Kenyan claimants for £19.9 million including costs, and agreed to fund a memorial in Nairobi.
https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2013-06-06/debates/13060646000005/MauMauClaims(Settlement)
stories.note: Research in progress: this card has no detainee's own words yet.

official.text: When I went out with the Askaris that morning I thought they would use batons against any prisoner refusing work without further instructions from me because I had been so instructed.
official.who: Hola camp's Chief Warder, a camp officer, in evidence at the coroner's inquest, as read out in the House of Commons by Dingle Foot MP
official.date: evidence at the 1959 inquest; read out 27 July 1959

official.text: I cannot accept his charge that this operation was likely to have serious, grave, or even tragic results. If the operation had been carried out as planned, that would not have been the consequence.
official.who: Alan Lennox-Boyd, Colonial Secretary, defending the government in the House of Commons

today.text: However, I would like to make it clear now and for the first time on behalf of Her Majesty's Government that we understand the pain and grievance felt by those who were involved in the events of the emergency in Kenya. The British Government recognise that Kenyans were subject to torture and other forms of ill treatment at the hands of the colonial administration. The British Government sincerely regret that these abuses took place and that they marred Kenya's progress towards independence. Torture and ill treatment are abhorrent violations of human dignity, which we unreservedly condemn.
today.who: William Hague, Foreign Secretary, statement to the House of Commons

disputed: How many were detained. Britannica gives more than 20,000 in one article and more than 70,000 Kikuyu in another; the BBC says some 150,000 went through screening.

How many died. Colonial figures counted more than 11,000 rebels killed, and some scholars put combat deaths above 20,000; the historian Caroline Elkins suggested as many as 300,000 Kikuyu may have died, critics say her estimate rests on thin census data, and the demographer John Blacker estimated about 50,000 deaths linked to the Emergency.
stories.blind: Most of the record is British: officials, Parliament and the files kept back for decades. The detainees' own accounts survive mainly in court testimony and oral histories, and many colonial files were destroyed before independence.
reading: Mau Mau claims settlement, House of Commons, 6 June 2013 (Hansard)
Hola Camp debate, House of Commons, 27 July 1959 (Hansard)

stories.title: Parihaka
facts: In 1865 the colonial government proclaimed the confiscation of a large part of Taranaki.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_land_confiscations
Parihaka was founded in 1866 as a final refuge for Taranaki hapū whose homes and crops Crown troops had repeatedly destroyed.
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2019/60/en/latest/
The West Coast Settlement (North Island) Act 1880 made pulling up survey pegs, ploughing and fencing punishable by up to two years in jail, with arrest allowed without a warrant.
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2019/60/en/latest/

More than 400 protesters were held as political prisoners, and laws allowed them to be kept in South Island jails without trial; an 1882 law provided that the leaders Te Whiti and Tohu would not be tried.
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2019/60/en/latest/
At dawn on 5 November 1881 about 1,600 troops and armed constabulary entered Parihaka.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parihaka

The Crown apologised to the people of Parihaka at a reconciliation ceremony, He Puanga Haeata, recorded in a deed signed on 9 June 2017; the Parihaka Reconciliation Act 2019 records that apology for invading Parihaka and forcibly evicting people who had sought refuge there.
https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2019/60/en/latest/

voices.text: Te Whiti when under arrest spoke to his people and asked them to be lionhearted and patient. He said "this is not my work but, comes from the hearts of the Europeans." Tohu followed and said "These are the doings of war. Be not sorry, turn away the sorrowful heart from you. We go away as fools. As mistaken men we looked for peace, and we find war. Be steadfast; keep to peaceful works; be not dismayed; have no fear."
voices.who: Te Whiti o Rongomai and Tohu Kākahi at their arrest, as reported in English translation
voices.doc: Taking Te Whiti, Tohu, & Hiroki (Papers Past)

witness.text: A portion of the fence had been removed to allow free access, and 500 loaves had been baked and were ready as a present to the troops. Te Whiti and Tohu received the Specials well, and gave them an empty whare close by from which they could hear and see everything. The natives did not seem at all alarmed, and were warned by Tohu and others that they must not offer any resistance no matter what happened. At 8-30 the troops began to surround the pah, and as they took up position the native children went out and danced a haka before them.
witness.who: Press Association reporters who entered Parihaka despite the minister's press ban

official.text: The Queen and the law must be supreme in Parihaka as well as elsewhere, and Te Whiti and his people are now called upon to accept the proposals made to them, which would give large and ample reserves to the people.
official.who: Proclamation by the Administrator of the Government, reprinted in the Thames Star (scanning errors corrected)

disputed: How many. The 1881 reporters counted about 1,500 people on the marae; later accounts give about 1,600 troops and say 1,600 people were driven out within weeks. The figures differ between sources.

How it was framed. In 1881 one newspaper headlined the government notice a proclamation of war; the Crown called it making the Queen and the law supreme; in 2019 the Crown said it had responded to peace with tyranny.
stories.blind: Almost every 1881 record was written by Pākehā reporters and officials and reaches us through interpreters' English; Parihaka's own account in te reo Māori is not in these sources.
reading: Parihaka Reconciliation Act 2019, with the Crown apology
The Taranaki Report: Kaupapa Tuatahi (Waitangi Tribunal, 1996)

stories.title: The siege and destruction of Melos
stories.where: Ancient city of Melos, near Plaka, island of Milos, Greece (approximate)
facts: Melos was a colony of Sparta that would not submit to Athens like the other Aegean islanders; Thucydides says it stayed neutral at first and turned openly hostile after Athens raided its land.
https://www.gutenberg.org/files/7142/7142-h/7142-h.htm

In the summer of 416 BC Athens sent 38 ships (30 Athenian, 6 Chian, 2 Lesbian) with about 3,100 heavy infantry, 300 archers and 20 mounted archers against the island; before fighting, its generals sent envoys, whom the Melian leaders received in private rather than before the people.
https://www.gutenberg.org/files/7142/7142-h/7142-h.htm

The Melians refused to become a tribute-paying ally, held out under siege and twice broke through part of the Athenian lines, but surrendered that winter after reinforcements came from Athens and some treachery inside the city.
https://www.gutenberg.org/files/7142/7142-h/7142-h.htm
Athens put the grown men to death, sold the women and children as slaves and settled 500 of its own colonists on the island.
https://www.gutenberg.org/files/7142/7142-h/7142-h.htm
After Athens lost the war, the Spartan commander Lysander restored the island to its Dorian possessors, but Britannica says it never recovered its prosperity.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Melos
The phrase "Melian famine" entered Greek as a byword for extreme starvation, first known in Aristophanes' Birds (414 BC), which suggests the city surrendered only after terrible hunger.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Melos

voices.text: To the fairness of quietly instructing each other as you propose there is nothing to object; but your military preparations are too far advanced to agree with what you say, as we see you are come to be judges in your own cause, and that all we can reasonably expect from this negotiation is war, if we prove to have right on our side and refuse to submit, and in the contrary case, slavery.
voices.who: The Melian commissioners, as recorded (and reconstructed) by the Athenian historian Thucydides
voices.doc: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5 (the Melian Dialogue), tr. Richard Crawley (1874)

voices.text: Well then, if you risk so much to retain your empire, and your subjects to get rid of it, it were surely great baseness and cowardice in us who are still free not to try everything that can be tried, before submitting to your yoke.
voices.who: The Melian commissioners, as recorded by Thucydides
voices.doc: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, tr. Richard Crawley (1874)

voices.text: You may be sure that we are as well aware as you of the difficulty of contending against your power and fortune, unless the terms be equal. But we trust that the gods may grant us fortune as good as yours, since we are just men fighting against unjust, and that what we want in power will be made up by the alliance of the Lacedaemonians, who are bound, if only for very shame, to come to the aid of their kindred. Our confidence, therefore, after all is not so utterly irrational.
voices.who: The Melian commissioners, as recorded by Thucydides
voices.doc: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, tr. Richard Crawley (1874)

voices.text: Our resolution, Athenians, is the same as it was at first. We will not in a moment deprive of freedom a city that has been inhabited these seven hundred years; but we put our trust in the fortune by which the gods have preserved it until now, and in the help of men, that is, of the Lacedaemonians; and so we will try and save ourselves. Meanwhile we invite you to allow us to be friends to you and foes to neither party, and to retire from our country after making such a treaty as shall seem fit to us both.
voices.who: The Melians' final answer to the Athenian envoys, as recorded by Thucydides
voices.doc: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, tr. Richard Crawley (1874)

witness.text: Reinforcements afterwards arriving from Athens in consequence, under the command of Philocrates, son of Demeas, the siege was now pressed vigorously; and some treachery taking place inside, the Melians surrendered at discretion to the Athenians, who put to death all the grown men whom they took, and sold the women and children for slaves, and subsequently sent out five hundred colonists and inhabited the place themselves.
witness.who: Thucydides, an Athenian (and former Athenian general, in exile at the time), closing his account of Melos without comment (tr. Richard Crawley, 1874)

witness.text: There was mourning and sorrow for those that were lost, but the lamentation for the dead was merged in even deeper sorrow for themselves, as they pictured the evils they were about to suffer, the like of which they themselves had inflicted upon the men of Melos, who were colonists of the Lacedaemonians, when they mastered them by siege.
witness.who: Xenophon, Hellenica, Book 2, describing Athens on the night news came of its defeat at Aegospotami (tr. H. G. Dakyns)

official.text: For ourselves, we shall not trouble you with specious pretences—either of how we have a right to our empire because we overthrew the Mede, or are now attacking you because of wrong that you have done us—and make a long speech which would not be believed; and in return we hope that you, instead of thinking to influence us by saying that you did not join the Lacedaemonians, although their colonists, or that you have done us no wrong, will aim at what is feasible, holding in view the real sentiments of us both; since you know as well as we do that right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
official.who: The Athenian envoys to Melos, as recorded by Thucydides (tr. Richard Crawley, 1874)

stories.warn: The Melian Dialogue is not a transcript. Thucydides, who was in exile and not present, says his speeches give what each occasion demanded of the speakers while keeping as closely as possible to the general sense of what was really said. The English is Richard Crawley's 1874 translation.
disputed: Were all the men killed? Thucydides says Athens put to death all the grown men it took, and Plutarch writes of the slaughter of all of military age; but Xenophon and Plutarch both say that in 405 BC Lysander restored the Melians to their island, and Wikipedia's summary of scholarship describes him restoring the survivors, so some Melians outlived the massacre, whether as enslaved captives, escapees or people absent at the time.

Who decided the massacre? Thucydides names no decree. Plutarch says Alcibiades spoke in favour of the decree and was the principal cause of the slaughter, and took a captive Melian woman, by whom he had a son; a speech falsely attributed to the orator Andocides also blames Alcibiades, but gives no date, and its authenticity and reliability are doubted.

Was Melos really neutral? Thucydides says it turned to open hostility after Athens raided it in 426 BC, and an inscription records some Melians giving silver to Sparta's war effort; but no ancient writer names a specific offence against Athens, and scholars generally regard Melos as an innocent victim of Athenian imperialism.

How Athenians later judged it. Xenophon records Athenians in 405 BC fearing the same treatment they gave Melos; the Athenian orator Isocrates admits Athens was reproached for enslaving the Melians but defends it as no worse than what other powers did.

Euripides' Trojan Women (March 415 BC), a play about the women of a conquered city. Britannica says the slaughter at Melos inspired it, and the scholar Neil Croally reads it as a reaction to Melos; the historian Mark Ringer thinks this unlikely, since the play was probably already in preparation before the siege began.
stories.blind: Every Melian word here reaches us through an Athenian historian who was not in the room and wrote the speeches himself to fit the occasion. No Melian account survives. The ordinary Melians, who were kept out of the talks, have no recorded words, and the women and children sold into slavery vanish from the record entirely.
reading: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, tr. Crawley (Project Gutenberg; the Melian Dialogue is in Book 5)

stories.title: The First Opium War
stories.where: Humen (the Bogue), on the Pearl River below Canton (Guangzhou), China (approximate)
facts: Foreign traders, mainly British, had been illegally exporting opium, mostly from India, to China since the 18th century; the trade grew dramatically from about 1820, and widespread addiction caused serious social and economic disruption in China.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Opium-Wars
In spring 1839 the Chinese government confiscated and destroyed more than 20,000 chests of opium, some 1,400 tons, that British merchants had warehoused at Canton.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Opium-Wars

To force the surrender, Lin Zexu confined the foreign merchants to their quarters in Canton, and the British Superintendent of Trade, Charles Elliot, persuaded them to hand over their opium on the promise that the British government would compensate them.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Opium_War

In July 1839 drunken British sailors killed a Chinese villager, and the British government, not wishing its subjects to be tried in the Chinese legal system, refused to hand the accused men over to Chinese courts.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Opium-Wars
A British expeditionary force arrived in June 1840, attacked the walled city of Canton in May 1841 and received a ransom of $6 million, and the fighting ended in August 1842 when Nanjing yielded.
https://www.britannica.com/place/China/The-first-Opium-War-and-its-aftermath

Under the Treaty of Nanking, signed on 29 August 1842, China ceded the Island of Hong Kong to Britain in perpetuity and agreed to pay 21 million dollars: 6 million for the opium surrendered in 1839, 3 million for debts owed by Chinese merchants and 12 million for Britain's costs of the war.
https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Nanking

The treaty opened five ports to British trade and residence instead of one, and a supplementary treaty in 1843 gave British subjects the right to be tried by British courts; Britannica dates the era of unequal treaties from these wars.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Opium-Wars

voices.text: We have heard that in your own country opium is prohibited with the utmost strictness and severity:—this is a strong proof that you know full well how hurtful it is to mankind. Since then you do not permit it to injure your own country, you ought not to have the injurious drug transferred to another country, and above all others, how much less to the Inner Land!
voices.who: Lin Zexu, the Qing imperial commissioner sent to Canton to suppress the opium trade, with his colleagues, in a letter to Queen Victoria (writing as an official of the state whose people were affected)
voices.doc: Letter to the queen of England, The Chinese Repository, vol. VIII, no. 10 (February 1840), p. 499, translated in the Canton Press (transcribed from the scan)

voices.text: Let us suppose that foreigners came from another country, and brought opium into England, and seduced the people of your country to smoke it, would not you, the sovereign of the said country, look upon such a procedure with anger, and in your just indignation endeavor to get rid of it? Now we have always heard that your highness possesses a most kind and benevolent heart, surely then you are incapable of doing or causing to be done unto another, that which you should not wish another to do unto you!
voices.who: Lin Zexu and colleagues, letter to Queen Victoria (writing as an official of the state whose people were affected)
voices.doc: The Chinese Repository, vol. VIII, no. 10 (February 1840), p. 500 (transcribed from the scan)

voices.text: Pause and reflect for a moment: if you foreigners did not bring the opium hither, where should our Chinese people get it to re-sell? It is you foreigners who involve our simple natives in the pit of death, and are they alone to be permitted to escape alive?
voices.who: Lin Zexu and colleagues, letter to Queen Victoria (writing as an official of the state whose people were affected)
voices.doc: The Chinese Repository, vol. VIII, no. 10 (February 1840), p. 501 (transcribed from the scan; OCR 'per- • fitted' read as 'permitted')

witness.text: They gave you notice to abandon your contraband trade. When they found that you would not, they had a right to drive you from their coasts on account of your obstinacy in persisting in this infamous and atrocious traffic. You allowed your agent to aid and abet those who were concerned in carrying on that trade, and I do not know how it can be urged as a crime against the Chinese that they refused provisions to those who refused obedience to their laws whilst residing within their territories. I am not competent to judge how long this war may last, or how protracted may be its operations, but this I can say, that a war more unjust in its origin, a war more calculated in its progress to cover this country with permanent disgrace, I do not know, and I have not read of.
witness.who: William Ewart Gladstone, opposition MP for Newark, speaking against the government in the House of Commons debate on the war with China (Hansard)

official.text: He would be the last to defend a trade which involved the violation of the municipal laws of the Chinese, and which furnished an enormously large population with the means of demoralization, which tended to the production of habits inconsistent with good order and correct conduct. But he put it to any man opposite, whether he could with a grave face say, that he honestly believed the motive of the Chinese government to have been the promotion of the growth of moral habits? The answer to such a supposition was, why did they not prohibit the growth of the poppy in their own country? The fact was, that this was an exportation of bullion question, an agricultural interest-protection question.
official.who: Viscount Palmerston, Foreign Secretary, defending the government in the House of Commons (Hansard reports his speech in the third person)

official.text: The Emperor of China agrees to pay the sum of Six Millions of Dollars as the value of the opium which was delivered up at Canton in the month of March, 1839, as a Ransom for the lives of Her Britannic Majesty’s Superintendent, and Subjects, who had been imprisoned and threatened with death by the Chinese High Officers.
official.who: Treaty of Nanking, Article 4, the peace terms Britain imposed at the end of the war

stories.warn: Lin Zexu was himself a senior Qing official writing for the emperor, not an ordinary Chinese subject. The English is the translation printed in the Canton Press and reprinted in The Chinese Repository in 1840; historians generally agree the letter never reached Queen Victoria.
disputed: Opium or trade and diplomatic equality? Britannica says the wars arose from China's attempts to suppress the opium trade, and Gladstone told the Commons the British flag was being hoisted to protect an infamous contraband traffic; on the other side, Palmerston argued the Qing were moved by the outflow of silver and their own poppy growers rather than morals, the British government insisted on free trade and equal diplomatic recognition, the historian Glenn Melancon argues the issue was not opium but Britain's honour and commitment to free trade, and John Quincy Adams called opium a mere incident and the kowtow the cause.

How the anti-opium campaign treated Chinese people. Lin's own letter says any Chinese who sold or merely smoked opium was liable to death, and he arrested about 1,700 Chinese dealers and smugglers on arrival in Canton; the campaign that resisted Britain was also harsh on China's own poor users and sellers.
stories.blind: The Chinese side survives here mostly in the words of officials, translated by foreigners for a foreign readership; the opium smokers, the boatmen and villagers along the Pearl River and the soldiers who died defending the forts left almost no records of their own in English. The British record is full, from Hansard to the treaty, and includes its own dissenters.
reading: The Chinese Repository, vol. VIII, with Lin's letter (Internet Archive)
House of Commons debate on the war with China, 1840 (Hansard)
